Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models

The math that prices a stock option is the math that helps generate images — Wall Street to AI labs, same machinery, different century.

Itô’s lemma yields both the Black-Scholes equation and DDPM’s forward diffusion process from one rule, (dW)² = dt — a rigorous, self-contained tour of stochastic calculus connecting quantitative finance and generative AI.
Author

Date Title
Aug 10, 2026 Itô's Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models — you are here
Sep 10, 2026 Variational Bounds and Score Matching: Two Routes to Denoising Diffusion

The first time I saw the forward process of a diffusion model written as an SDE by Song et al. [1], what struck me was not the idea but the notation. Change a few words — "noise schedule" for "volatility" — and it was an equation I had solved many times before. The process is presented as something new — a device for training image generators that adds a little Gaussian noise step after step until the data dissolves into pure noise. But the equation underneath was one I had spent years with in a different domain. I had seen that drift-plus-noise structure before; I had taken that same N \to \infty limit before; I had used that same lemma to reduce a state-dependent SDE to one I could solve.

That lemma is Itô’s. In quantitative finance it is the engine behind the Black-Scholes equation: feed it a stochastic stock price, hedge away the randomness, and a deterministic PDE for the option’s fair value remains. In a diffusion model it performs two operations that look unrelated — applied one way it turns the noised state into a Gaussian that can be sampled in a single step; applied another it yields a PDE for how that noise spreads. Same lemma, two fields, half a century apart.

What connects them is a single rule of stochastic calculus, (dW)^2 = dt — the one fact for which ordinary calculus has no term. Pricing derivatives, I had taken its consequences for granted. In image generation, the very same correction term reappears at the heart of the diffusion machinery. This post builds that rule from first principles and then applies it three times: to derive the Black-Scholes equation, to give the DDPM forward process its closed-form perturbation kernel, and to derive that process’s Fokker-Planck equation. One identity, carried to two ends of a bridge that quantitative finance and generative AI did not know they shared.

Roadmap

This post is structured in six parts:

  • Part 1: Develops Brownian motion — the foundational random process underlying all the SDEs in this series.
  • Part 2: Introduces SDEs and Itô’s lemma — the calculus that turns Brownian inputs into derived processes.
  • Part 3: Derives the Black-Scholes equation using Itô’s lemma — the canonical application from quantitative finance.
  • Part 4: Shows that the forward process of DDPM [2], formulated as an SDE [1], is the same machinery applied to different questions.
  • Part 5: Draws the three derivations together — Black-Scholes, the perturbation kernel, and the Fokker-Planck equation — comparing the effect of the Itô correction on each.
  • Part 6: Discusses why this unification matters — for ML practitioners and for quants.

1 Brownian Motion

Part 1 begins with a glimpse of Brownian motion’s physics along with the two complementary views to see it. After that it constructs Brownian motion from first principles: first its defining properties, then the quadratic variation that measures a path’s accumulated squared fluctuation and reveals Brownian motion as continuous yet nowhere differentiable. That roughness is not incidental; it is the reason ordinary calculus fails here and a new one is required. Made precise, it yields the rule (dW)^2 = dt, the single identity on which the entire Itô calculus of Part 2 — and the SDEs of everything after — rests.

1.1 The physics

In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown watched particles released from pollen grains jitter randomly in water [3]. In 1905 Einstein explained it [4]: invisible water molecules bombard the particle, and the accumulation of countless random collisions produces a random, continuous path (Figure 1).

The mathematics describing such a path — and, crucially, describing how the probability of finding the particle at each location spreads over time — comes in two complementary forms: an equation for the random trajectory of one particle (the Langevin equation [5]), and an equation for the evolving probability cloud of where it might be (the Fokker-Planck equation). These two views — one trajectory, one distribution — are the same physics seen two ways (Figure 2).

That duality recurs through this entire blog series. In Part 2 of this first post it reappears as the two ways of applying Itô’s lemma: Pattern A follows the trajectory, Pattern B tracks the density (Section 2.3).

1.2 Definition

Brownian motion is the mathematical idealization of that path (Figure 1). It is the continuum limit of a random walk, as the steps shrink toward zero and grow infinitely frequent (Appendix A.1). Computing with it — integrating against it, transforming it, building SDEs on it — needs more than the informal picture, so the properties below specify the object precisely.

It is the foundational random process of continuous-time stochastic calculus — the noise source of every SDE in this series, from the stock-price models of Parts 2–3 to the diffusion-model forward process of Part 4 — and its defining surprise is a path that is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere.

Formally, a standard Brownian motion (or Wiener process) is a stochastic process W_t on [0, \infty) satisfying:

  1. W_0 = 0
  2. For 0 \le s < t, the increment W_t - W_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, t - s)
  3. Increments over non-overlapping intervals are independent
  4. The sample paths t \mapsto W_t are continuous (almost surely)

The properties imply a non-obvious fact: although W_t is continuous, its sample paths are not differentiable (Figure 3). The route to it, and the ground of every later rule of Itô calculus, is the quadratic variation of W. What it delivers is that no continuously differentiable path survives; the stronger statement, that the paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable, is a theorem of Paley, Wiener and Zygmund [6], quoted in the geometric interpretation below.

1.3 Quadratic variation

Quadratic variation is the one quantity that distinguishes ordinary smooth functions from Brownian motion — and so identifies where differentiability fails. We define it first for an arbitrary continuous function, deliberately making no smoothness or randomness assumptions, and then evaluate that definition in the two cases that follow: a C^1 function (continuously differentiable — one with a continuous first derivative), where it collapses to zero, and a Brownian path, where it does not.

For a continuous, real-valued function g: [0, t] \to \mathbb{R} and a partition \Pi: 0 = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = t with increments \Delta t_i = t_{i+1} - t_i and mesh \|\Pi\| = \max_{0 \le i \le n-1} \Delta t_i, the quadratic variation of g on [0, t] is

\boxed{[g]_t \;=\; \lim_{\|\Pi\| \to 0} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2} \tag{1}

when the limit exists.

1.4 Smooth functions have zero quadratic variation

Before turning to W, we compute [g]_t for a smooth function as a baseline — it will vanish, and tracking why is what later determines what makes Brownian motion different. Each increment of a C^1 function is of order \Delta t_i, so its square is of order (\Delta t_i)^2 — one power of the mesh too small to survive the sum.

If g \in C^1 with |g'| \le M on [0, t] (where M = \max_{s \in [0, t]} |g'(s)|), then for some \tau_i \in (t_i, t_{i+1}) the mean-value theorem applied on each subinterval gives

g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i) \;=\; g'(\tau_i)\,(t_{i+1} - t_i)

Squaring,

\big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;=\; \big(g'(\tau_i)\big)^2 (\Delta t_i)^2

Using |g'| \le M,

\big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;\le\; M^2 (\Delta t_i)^2

Summing across the partition,

\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;\le\; M^2 \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\, \Delta t_i since \Delta t_i \le \|\Pi\|,

\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;\le\; M^2\, \|\Pi\| \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \Delta t_i

Telescoping \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \Delta t_i = t,

\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;\le\; M^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \big(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i)\big)^2 \;\le\; M^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

So the partition sum is squeezed to zero — smooth functions have [g]_t = 0.

1.5 Brownian motion has quadratic variation t

The smooth case was deterministic; this one is not. In Section 1.4 the mean-value theorem fixed each increment at a definite value, so the partition sum was an ordinary number we could squeeze to zero. For Brownian motion there is no mean-value theorem — W is nowhere differentiable — and the increments \Delta W_i = W_{t_{i+1}} - W_{t_i} are random, which makes the sum S = \sum_i (\Delta W_i)^2 itself a random variable.

Thus, a pointwise squeeze is unavailable and “[W]_t” must be read as a probabilistic limit. So we show S concentrates on a single deterministic value in L^2 (i.e. in mean square: \mathbb{E}[(S - t)^2] \to 0), in four steps:

  1. Compute its mean (linearity of expectation, telescoping to t)
  2. Compute its variance (Gaussian fourth moments, plus independent increments so variances add)
  3. Shrink the mesh to send the variance to 0 via the same inequality \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\,t as before, the difference being that it now eliminates a variance, not the sum itself
  4. Conclude that mean t with vanishing variance forces S \to t

For W_t, each increment satisfies \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t_i) — the common starting point for all four steps.

Step 1 — the mean:

By linearity of expectation,

\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \mathbb{E}\!\big[(\Delta W_i)^2\big]

Substituting \mathbb{E}[(\Delta W_i)^2] = \Delta t_i (each \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t_i) is mean-zero, so its second moment equals its variance \Delta t_i),

\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \Delta t_i

Telescoping \sum_i \Delta t_i = t,

\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;=\; t

Step 2 — the variance:

The increments are independent, so variances add across the sum,

\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \operatorname{Var}\!\big((\Delta W_i)^2\big)

Substituting \operatorname{Var}\!\big((\Delta W_i)^2\big) = 2(\Delta t_i)^2, since \operatorname{Var}(X^2) = \mathbb{E}[X^4] - \big(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\big)^2 = 3\sigma^4 - \sigma^4 for X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) (with \mathbb{E}[X^4] = 3\sigma^4: write X = \sigma Z, and one Gaussian integration by parts gives \mathbb{E}[Z^4] = 3),

\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;=\; 2\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta t_i)^2

Step 3 — shrink the mesh:

Applying the mesh inequality \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\, t,

\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\Delta W_i)^2\right] \;\le\; 2\,\|\Pi\|\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\|\to 0}\; 0

Step 4 — conclude:

The partition sum has mean t and variance vanishing to zero, so it converges in L^2 to the deterministic limit:

\boxed{\,[W]_t \;=\; t\,} \tag{2}

The quadratic variation of Brownian motion on [0, t] is exactly t, not zero — a structural property of W, not an artifact of any specific partition. \square

1.5.1 Where smoothness made the difference

Both derivations look structurally similar — square the increment, sum across the partition, apply the mesh inequality — yet the smooth sum collapses to 0 while the Brownian sum lands on t.

For the smooth function, the mean-value theorem and squaring allowed us to take M^2 out as a factor. As the expression was degree 2 in \Delta t_i, one factor of \Delta t_i was absorbed by the mesh inequality and the other telescoped to t; once the limit \|\Pi\| \to 0 was applied, we found that [g]_t = 0.

For Brownian motion, W isn’t differentiable, so we cannot apply the mean-value theorem and take M^2 out as a factor. Instead, the increments \Delta W_i being random made the sum S = \sum_i (\Delta W_i)^2 itself a random variable, which forced us to take the mean-variance route. The variance vanished, eliminated by the mesh inequality as the smooth sum was, because it carries (\Delta t_i)^2. The mean did not, because \mathbb{E}[(\Delta W_i)^2] = \Delta t_i leaves it degree 1 in \Delta t_i, and a degree-1 sum telescopes to t instead of vanishing. That single power difference is the whole story:

The smooth case has an extra \Delta t_i per term that the mesh inequality absorbs — one factor becomes \|\Pi\|, the other telescopes to t, net bound M^2\,\|\Pi\|\,t \to 0. The Brownian case has only one factor of \Delta t_i per term, so the sum telescopes to t directly, with no extra \Delta t_i left for the mesh inequality to absorb. Differentiability buys that one extra power of \Delta t_i, and that one extra power is what makes the sum vanish.

1.6 Geometric interpretation of why [W]_t = t makes Brownian motion non-differentiable

The quadratic-variation results of the previous sections have a vivid geometric reading. A function’s local smoothness is what a magnifying glass reveals: zoom far enough into a differentiable curve and it looks like a straight line — its tangent — whereas zoom into a Brownian path and it stays as irregular as ever. The two subsections below make this contrast precise, and it is the same contrast that decides whether a squared increment survives in the limit.

1.6.1 Smooth functions

A differentiable function has a well-defined slope at every point. Geometrically that means it is locally linear: over a small step \Delta t its increment is f'(t)\,\Delta t = O(\Delta t), proportional to the step. Take even a high-curvature region and zoom in, and the curve bends less and less, settling toward its tangent line (Figure 4). For f twice differentiable, the departure from the tangent over a window of width \Delta t is the curvature term \tfrac{1}{2} f''\,(\Delta t)^2 = O(\Delta t^2) — it shrinks faster than the window, so the squared increment is negligible next to \Delta t, which is why a smooth path has zero quadratic variation.

The magnified curve is shallower but not perfectly straight — a slight bend remains at finite zoom, and zooming further would reduce it further still, approaching a straight line in the limit. Because the bend shrinks this way, the squared increment is negligible: (\Delta f)^2 = O(\Delta t^2) \to 0 relative to \Delta t. This is the geometric face of the zero quadratic variation derived in Section 1.4. Brownian motion, we will now see, refuses to straighten.

1.6.2 Brownian motion

The quadratic-variation result [W]_t = t (Equation 2) is the algebraic statement that a Brownian increment scales as \Delta W \sim \sqrt{\Delta t}. That square-root scaling has an immediate geometric consequence: the slope of a chord over a step is \Delta W / \Delta t \sim 1/\sqrt{\Delta t} \to \infty as \Delta t \to 0, so the difference quotient blows up rather than converging to a finite slope, and the path is not continuously differentiable. In fact a classical theorem of Paley, Wiener and Zygmund [6] establishes the stronger property that Brownian paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable; the scaling here is the intuition behind that result, not a proof of it. Figure 5 makes this visible through statistical self-similarity [7]: zooming into any sub-interval and rescaling by the same \sqrt{\Delta t} law reproduces a path just as irregular as the original, so there is no scale at which the path ever straightens out.

The same \sqrt{\Delta t} scaling is what makes a squared increment matter. A smooth curve flattens toward its tangent under magnification, so its increment is O(\Delta t) and its square O(\Delta t^2) — negligible. The Brownian path never flattens: its increment is O(\sqrt{\Delta t}), so its square is O(\Delta t), the same order as dt itself. That is the content of [W]_t = t, and it is why a squared Brownian increment cannot be discarded — the fact we turn into a precise calculus rule in the next section.

1.7 The (dW)^2 = dt rule

What Equation 2 says at the level of infinitesimals is that (\Delta W)^2 behaves, in sum, like \Delta t. This is the meaning of the working rule

\boxed{(dW)^2 = dt} \tag{3}

— not a literal pointwise equality of random variables, but a calculus rule for what sums of (\Delta W)^2 terms converge to inside an integral.

1.7.1 What the rule means inside an integral

The precise content of Equation 3 is an integral statement. For any bounded, Riemann-integrable deterministic function f on [0, t] (continuous suffices),

\boxed{\int_0^t f(s)\,(dW_s)^2 \;:=\; \lim_{\|\Pi\| \to 0} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2 \;=\; \int_0^t f(s)\, ds} \tag{4}

with convergence in L^2 — the same calculation that gave [W]_t = t, now carrying the weight f.

Mean: By linearity of expectation,

\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big] \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)\, \mathbb{E}\big[(\Delta W_i)^2\big]

Substituting \mathbb{E}\big[(\Delta W_i)^2\big] = \Delta t_i,

\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big] \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0 (a Riemann sum),

\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big] \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; \int_0^t f(s)\, ds

Variance: By independence the variances add,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;=\; \sum_i \operatorname{Var}\big(f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\big)

Taking each deterministic factor out squared,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, \operatorname{Var}\big((\Delta W_i)^2\big)

Substituting \operatorname{Var}\big((\Delta W_i)^2\big) = 2(\Delta t_i)^2,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;=\; 2 \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, (\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding f(t_i)^2 \le \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;\le\; 2\big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2 \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\, t by the mesh,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;\le\; 2\big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;\le\; 2\big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

A random variable whose mean converges to \int_0^t f(s)\, ds and whose variance vanishes converges in L^2 to that limit, since \mathbb{E}\big[(S - \int_0^t f\, ds)^2\big] = \operatorname{Var}(S) + \big(\mathbb{E}[S] - \int_0^t f\, ds\big)^2 and both terms vanish. So the sum converges to \int_0^t f(s)\, ds — which is the value Equation 4 asserts. \square Setting f \equiv 1 specializes it to the plain quadratic variation Equation 2. So whenever (dW)^2 appears inside a stochastic integral with a deterministic weight, we may substitute dt for it, and the two integrals agree in the limit. Itô’s lemma will apply the rule with a random weight that depends only on the path up to that time. The same mean-and-variance argument goes through conditionally on that past, since the increment \Delta W_i is independent of it.

1.7.2 Companion rules

Two further rules,

\boxed{(dt)^2 = 0} \tag{5}

\boxed{dt\,dW = 0} \tag{6}

follow by the same partition-sum reasoning, established next.

1.7.2.1 The (dt)^2 rule is deterministic

This rule carries no randomness, so a single deterministic bound suffices — but the weight f may change sign, so the bound must control the sum in absolute value. By the triangle inequality,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \sum_i |f(t_i)|\,(\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding the weight by |f(t_i)| \le \sup_{[0,t]}|f|,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big) \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\, t by the mesh,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)\, \|\Pi\|\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)\, \|\Pi\|\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

The bound is deterministic — no randomness enters — and it squeezes the partition sum to zero in absolute value as the mesh refines, so the sum itself converges to zero, giving the integral form

\int_0^t f(s)\,(ds)^2 = 0

whose equivalent differential form is (dt)^2 = 0, Equation 5.

1.7.2.2 The dt\,dW rule is an L^2 statement

The partition sum \sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i has mean zero, since each \Delta W_i is mean-zero. For its variance, the increments are independent across non-overlapping intervals, so variances add,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;=\; \sum_i \operatorname{Var}\big(f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\big)

Taking each deterministic factor out squared,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, (\Delta t_i)^2\, \operatorname{Var}(\Delta W_i)

Substituting \operatorname{Var}(\Delta W_i) = \Delta t_i,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, (\Delta t_i)^3

Bounding f(t_i)^2 \le \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2 \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^3

Bounding two of the three factors of each (\Delta t_i)^3 by the mesh, (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|^2,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|^2 \sum_i \Delta t_i

Telescoping \sum_i \Delta t_i = t,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|^2\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|^2\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

The partition sum thus has mean zero and a variance vanishing to zero as the mesh refines. A sequence with mean zero whose variance tends to zero converges to zero in L^2, so the partition sum converges in L^2 to zero, giving the integral form

\int_0^t f(s)\, ds\, dW_s = 0

whose equivalent differential form is dt\,dW = 0, Equation 6.

So only (dW)^2 survives at first order in dt — and what survives, by Equation 4, is dt.

1.8 The Itô integral: a Gaussian under L^2

The same partition-sum construction determines one more object used throughout: the Itô integral of a deterministic function against Brownian motion, \int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s := \lim_{\|\Pi\| \to 0} \sum_i g(t_i)\, \Delta W_i — the left-endpoint limit of partition sums, as in Equation 4 but now linear in \Delta W_i instead of (\Delta W_i)^2. Defining it rigorously for general random integrands is carried out in Appendix A.4 [7]; the deterministic case is all the closed-form solutions of this post need, and there the Wiener increment structure alone fixes the full distribution. The Fokker-Planck derivation of Part 4 uses one property of the random case, its zero mean, and takes it from that appendix.

For deterministic g,

\boxed{\int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\;\; \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds\right)} \tag{7}

Why: Approximate the integral by a partition sum \sum_i g(t_i)\, \Delta W_i, with independent increments \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t_i). A finite linear combination of independent Gaussians is Gaussian, so each partition sum is Gaussian; its mean vanishes term by term, and by independence its variance is \sum_i g(t_i)^2\, \Delta t_i \to \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds (a Riemann sum, g continuous).

As \|\Pi\| \to 0 the sums converge in L^2 to the integral, because each partition sum is the integral of a step function, and those integrals form a Cauchy sequence in L^2 as the mesh refines — the construction carried out in Appendix A.4. Because L^2 convergence carries the mean and variance to the limit, the limit has mean 0 and variance \int_0^t g^2\, ds; and a mean-square limit of Gaussians is itself Gaussian — the Gaussian family is closed under L^2 limits, proved in Appendix A.6 — so the integral is Gaussian. The variance identity is the Itô isometry; the zero mean follows from the martingale property of the Itô integral.

Martingale property: (made precise in Appendix A.5) A martingale is a process with no systematic trend — given everything observed up to the present, its expected future value equals its present value. The Itô integral M_t = \int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s is one, and since it starts at M_0 = 0, taking expectations gives \mathbb{E}[M_t] = 0 for every t — on average it neither rises nor falls. This is the zero-mean half of Equation 7.

Itô isometry: An isometry is a map that preserves size. The map g \mapsto \int_0^t g\, dW_s sends a function to a random variable while preserving the L^2 norm: \mathbb{E}\big[\big(\int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s\big)^2\big] = \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds — the mean-square size of the integral equals the ordinary size of the integrand. This is the variance half of Equation 7.

2 SDEs and Itô’s Lemma

Brownian motion is undirected noise — a continuous but nowhere-differentiable path whose only quantitative descriptor is its quadratic variation [W]_t = t, expressed in the working rule (dW)^2 = dt. On its own it has zero drift and a fixed, state-independent variance rate, so it models no particular system; this part builds state-dependent processes from it. First, SDEs define the process — a drift term that adds deterministic direction, a diffusion term that scales the noise — and then Itô’s lemma gives the calculus for transforming such processes, with the surviving (dW)^2 = dt correction doing all the work. Together they are the engine we run in Parts 3 and 4.

2.1 Stochastic differential equations

Brownian motion is pure, undirected noise — mean-zero increments whose variance accumulates at unit rate (Equation 2). Real systems rarely behave so simply: a stock price exhibits a trend, a temperature relaxes toward ambient, a population grows — each carrying its own deterministic tendency while still being buffeted by randomness, often responding to that noise with an intensity that depends on the current state. To describe such a process we specify not its value but its instantaneous change — a deterministic push over dt plus a scaled increment of W_t — and let those infinitesimal updates accumulate into a path.

A (one-dimensional) Itô stochastic differential equation (SDE) has the form

\boxed{dX_t = \mu(X_t, t)\, dt + \sigma(X_t, t)\, dW_t} \tag{8}

where \mu is the drift coefficient and \sigma is the diffusion coefficient. The notation dX_t, dt, dW_t is shorthand for the integral equation

\boxed{X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t \mu(X_s, s)\, ds + \int_0^t \sigma(X_s, s)\, dW_s} \tag{9}

where the second integral is the Itô integral of Section 1.8. There the integrand is deterministic; here \sigma(X_s, s) is generally state-dependent and therefore random, but the same heuristic form is all that is needed here.

The drift term governs the deterministic evolution of X_t; the diffusion term governs the size of random fluctuations. Conditions under which such an SDE has a unique solution — global Lipschitz and linear growth on \mu and \sigma — are stated, with a proof sketch, in Appendix A.1 of post #3; every process in this post satisfies them, and post #3 states the conditions its learned reverse-time drift must meet.

The next two subsections introduce two concrete instances of this form — geometric Brownian motion (GBM) and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process — each obtained by choosing the drift and diffusion coefficients \mu(x,t) and \sigma(x,t). We solve both later with Itô’s lemma (GBM in Section 2.4.1, the OU process in Section 2.4.2), and both recur downstream: the former as the Black-Scholes stock model in Part 3, the latter as the template for the DDPM forward process in Part 4.

2.1.1 Geometric Brownian motion

In the Black-Scholes framework, S_t denotes the price of a stock at time t, and is modeled by the SDE

\boxed{dS_t \;=\; \mu\, S_t\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t} \tag{10}

with scalar constants \mu, \sigma. This is Equation 8 with drift coefficient \mu(x, t) = \mu\, x and diffusion coefficient \sigma(x, t) = \sigma\, x — both linear in x. (The symbols \mu, \sigma are reused here as scalar constants, distinct from the coefficient functions \mu(x,t), \sigma(x,t) of Equation 8 — standard finance notation.)

The parameters have precise finance meanings:

  • Drift (\mu): The instantaneous expected rate of return per unit time, \mathbb{E}[dS_t/S_t] = \mu\, dt. \mu = 0.15 means a 15\% per-year expected return (with t measured in years); the continuously-compounded growth rate is the smaller \mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 (the Itô correction, derived below).
  • Volatility (\sigma): The standard deviation of the return per unit time. \sigma = 0.20 means 20\% per-year volatility.

Sample paths trend upward in expectation while remaining strictly positive (Figure 6). We solve this SDE for the full distribution of S_t — applying Itô’s lemma to \log S_t — in Section 2.4.1, where the price is shown to be lognormally distributed.

2.1.2 Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process

The OU process [8] is the canonical mean-reverting SDE. With state X_t \in \mathbb{R}, long-run mean \bar\mu, mean-reversion rate \kappa > 0, and constant volatility \sigma > 0,

\boxed{dX_t \;=\; \kappa\,(\bar\mu - X_t)\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, dW_t} \tag{11}

This is Equation 8 with drift coefficient \kappa(\bar\mu - x) (linear in x, restoring toward \bar\mu) and constant diffusion \sigma (independent of x).

The parameters:

  • Long-run mean (\bar\mu): The value the process is pulled toward.
  • Mean-reversion rate (\kappa): Units 1/\text{time}; larger \kappa pulls harder. The expected excursion decays as e^{-\kappa t} (Equation 17, derived in Section 2.4.2), so its “half-life” — the time to halve — is \ln 2 / \kappa.
  • Volatility (\sigma): The constant volatility of the noise, units \text{state}/\sqrt{\text{time}}.

The mean-reversion intuition: If X_t > \bar\mu, the drift \kappa(\bar\mu - X_t) < 0 pushes X_t back down. If X_t < \bar\mu, the drift pushes it back up. The noise term \sigma\, dW_t keeps the process jittering around \bar\mu rather than converging to it (Figure 7).

Stationary distribution: Unlike GBM — whose spread grows without bound (its log-return variance is \sigma^2 t, derived in Section 2.4.1) — OU has a finite-variance equilibrium. As t \to \infty,

\boxed{X_t \;\xrightarrow{\text{dist}}\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\bar\mu,\;\, \frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}\right)} \tag{12}

The equilibrium variance \sigma^2/(2\kappa) arises from the balance between noise injection (\sigma) and restoring force (\kappa): more noise widens the spread, stronger reversion tightens it. The full derivation — solving the SDE by an integrating factor and letting t \to \infty — is in Section 2.4.2 after Itô’s lemma is introduced.

Where OU shows up:

  • In finance:
    • In interest-rate modeling, the Vasicek model [9] treats the instantaneous risk-free rate as an OU process.
    • In statistical-arbitrage, cointegrated price spreads — the difference between two related instruments — are modeled as mean-reverting OU processes.
  • In generative AI:
    • OU is the simplest non-trivial Langevin-style SDE: it samples its Gaussian equilibrium \mathcal{N}(\bar\mu,\, \sigma^2/(2\kappa)) by mean reversion plus noise, and the same drift-plus-noise template lets Langevin dynamics sample any target distribution with a differentiable log-density (post #5).
    • The reverse, generative process of DDPM is that template generalized — a learned, time-dependent score \nabla_x \log p_t replaces OU’s fixed linear drift, turning pure noise back into data (post #3).

2.2 Itô’s lemma

The SDEs of Section 2.1 describe how a state X_t evolves; the question of interest is how functions of that state move. Given dX_t = \mu\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t, what SDE governs a transformed quantity Y_t = f(X_t, t) — a log-price, an option value, a rescaled noised state? For a smooth, deterministic X the ordinary chain rule would answer at once, but it fails here: the (dW)^2 = dt rule of Equation 3 means a second-order term that classical calculus discards instead survives at order dt. Itô’s lemma resolves this — it is the ordinary chain rule plus exactly one correction term.

Let X_t satisfy the SDE dX_t = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW_t, and let f(x, t) be a function that is twice continuously differentiable in x and once in t. Then according to Itô’s lemma the process Y_t = f(X_t, t) satisfies [10]

\boxed{df = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \mu \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right) dt + \sigma \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW} \tag{13}

The term \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, dt is the Itô correction. It is what distinguishes Itô calculus from ordinary calculus.

2.2.1 Derivation

Taylor-expand f(X_{t+dt}, t+dt) to second order in x and first order in t — all the smoothness f is assumed to possess; the omitted higher terms are of order dt \cdot dX and (dt)^2, which the companion rules Equation 6 and Equation 5 annihilate. The remainder of the second-order expansion is o\big((dX)^2\big), and (dX)^2 is itself of order dt, so the remainder contributes nothing at order dt:

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dX \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, (dX)^2

Substituting dX = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,(\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, (\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW)^2

Expanding the square,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,(\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\,\bigl(\mu^2 (dt)^2 + 2\mu\sigma\, dt\, dW + \sigma^2 (dW)^2\bigr)

Reducing the squared increment via the companion rules (dt)^2 = 0, dt\,dW = 0, (dW)^2 = dt,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,(\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, dt

Distributing \partial f / \partial x across the bracket,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, dt

Grouping by dt and dW gives,

\boxed{df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW}

which is Equation 13. \square

2.2.2 Comparison to the chain rule

Suppose we naively applied the ordinary chain rule to a stochastic X with dX = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW — substitute dX, stop at first order as we do in the ordinary case. We’d write

df \;\stackrel{?}{=}\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW

That is what ordinary calculus would give — and in Itô calculus it is the wrong answer. Itô’s lemma is character-for-character the same, except for one extra term in the dt coefficient:

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;+\; \underbrace{\boxed{\tfrac{1}{2}\,\sigma^2\,\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}}}_{\text{Itô correction — the square term}}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW

The boxed second-order term is the only structural difference between the two equations. Every other character matches the naive chain rule. It is the surviving term from the (dW)^2 = dt rule of Equation 3 — that partition-sum identity, promoted to a calculus correction.

2.2.3 The deterministic limit (\sigma \to 0)

A correct stochastic chain rule must reduce to the ordinary one when the noise is switched off — that is the sanity check.

Set \sigma = 0. The SDE loses its diffusion term,

dX_t = \mu\, dt

so X is now a smooth (differentiable) path with derivative \dot X = dX_t / dt = \mu.

For a smooth path, Y_t = f(X_t, t) changes for two reasons: f depends on t directly, and it depends on t through X_t. The ordinary multivariable chain rule sums the two contributions — the explicit rate \partial f / \partial t, and the rate transmitted through X moving at speed \dot X, namely \dot X\, \partial f / \partial x:

\frac{dY}{dt} \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \dot X\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}

Substituting \dot X = \mu,

\frac{dY}{dt} \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}

Multiplying by dt,

dY \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) dt

Now set \sigma = 0 in Itô’s lemma. Starting from the full result,

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW

Setting \sigma = 0 — the second-order term \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \partial^2 f / \partial x^2 and the \sigma\, \partial f / \partial x\, dW term both vanish —

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) dt

The two agree exactly: with no noise, Itô’s lemma is the ordinary chain rule. The second-order term is what the (dW)^2 = dt rule adds once \sigma \neq 0.

Thus, Itô’s lemma = ordinary chain rule + (dW)^2 = dt correction.

2.3 Application patterns of Itô’s lemma

Two patterns will recur. In one, we follow the path a particle takes once it starts moving; in the other, we track the probability-density cloud, estimating how likely the particle is to be at a given place and time after its journey begins. Specifically, Pattern A rides along a single trajectory: it transforms one SDE into another, tracking some function of the moving state. Pattern B steps back to ask, at each time and place, how likely the state is to be there: it turns the SDE into a partial differential equation (PDE) for the probability density. Same lemma, same SDE — one follows the path, the other predicts the distribution. These are the two views of one diffusion introduced in Section 1.1, now made into two ways of applying the lemma.

Pattern A: Given an SDE for X_t, derive an SDE for a transformed quantity f(X_t, t). It recurs in every part that follows:

  • Section 2.4.1: f(S) = \log S applied to the GBM stock price gives its closed-form lognormal distribution.
  • Section 2.4.2: The integrating-factor transform f(Z, t) = e^{\kappa t} Z applied to the long-run-mean-centered OU process gives its closed-form Gaussian distribution.
  • Section 3.3 – Section 3.7: f = V(S, t) applied to the GBM stock price yields the Black-Scholes PDE.
  • Section 4.9: A similar integrating-factor transform f(x, t) = x / \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} applied to the DDPM VP-SDE turns it into a driftless process, giving its closed-form Gaussian law — the perturbation kernel.

Pattern B: Given an SDE for X_t, derive a PDE for its probability density p(x, t) — the Fokker-Planck equation. It appears once:

  • Section 4.10: Applying Itô to a test function and taking expectations turns the VP-SDE into the Fokker-Planck equation for its marginal distribution p(x, t), giving the PDE that governs how the DDPM forward process spreads the data density into noise over time.

2.4 Itô’s lemma solves GBM and the OU process

Itô’s lemma is most convincing in action. We turn it on the two example SDEs from Section 2.1 — GBM and the OU process — and in each case a single application collapses a state-dependent SDE into one we can integrate in closed form.

2.4.1 Solving GBM

We solve GBM for the full distribution of the price S_t by applying Itô’s lemma to the transform f(S) = \log S — a function of S alone, with no explicit time dependence. (\log S requires S_t > 0, so the step is valid while the price stays positive; the resulting solution Equation 14 is an exponential, strictly positive for all t, and applying Itô’s lemma to it recovers Equation 10, so it solves the SDE with no assumption on the sign. Uniqueness of the solution under the conditions of Section 2.1 makes it the solution, which discharges the assumption.)

2.4.1.1 Use Itô to get reduced SDE

The SDE: The price S_t follows the GBM SDE Equation 10,

dS_t \;=\; \mu\, S_t\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t

Itô’s lemma: To avoid clashing with the GBM constants \mu, \sigma, write the generic lemma with drift coefficient a and diffusion coefficient b — that is, for a transform f(S_t, t) of a process dS_t = a\, dt + b\, dW_t, the lemma Equation 13 reads

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; a\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, b^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; b\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial S}\, dW

To apply it to f = \log S we need two elements: the coefficients a, b — identified from the GBM equation — and the partials of f — computed from f = \log S. We collect each, then substitute.

Coefficients (from the GBM equation): a = \mu\, S_t and b = \sigma\, S_t.

Partials (from f = \log S):

\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;=\; 0, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial S} \;=\; \frac{1}{S}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial S^2} \;=\; -\frac{1}{S^2}

Substituting a = \mu\, S, b = \sigma\, S, and the three partials into the lemma,

d(\log S_t) \;=\; \left(0 \;+\; (\mu\, S) \cdot \frac{1}{S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, (\sigma\, S)^2 \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{S^2}\right)\right) dt \;+\; (\sigma\, S) \cdot \frac{1}{S}\, dW_t

Simplifying,

d(\log S_t) \;=\; \left(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right) dt + \sigma\, dW_t

a constant-drift, constant-diffusion SDE: both coefficients are independent of S_t.

2.4.1.2 Solve reduced SDE by integration

Integrating this reduced SDE over [0, t],

\log\!\left(\frac{S_t}{S_0}\right) \;=\; \big(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\big)\, t \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t dW_s

Since W_0 = 0, the Itô integral is \int_0^t dW_s = W_t,

\boxed{\log\!\left(\frac{S_t}{S_0}\right) \;=\; \big(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\big)\, t \;+\; \sigma\, W_t} \tag{14}

2.4.1.3 Properties of the solution distribution

Since W_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t), the log-return is an affine function of a Gaussian — hence Gaussian:

\boxed{\log\!\left(\frac{S_t}{S_0}\right) \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\Big(\, \big(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\big)\, t,\;\; \sigma^2\, t \,\Big)} \tag{15}

Taking expectations of S_t = S_0\, e^{(\mu - \sigma^2/2)t + \sigma W_t}, with the deterministic factor pulled out,

\mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0\, e^{(\mu - \sigma^2/2)t}\, \mathbb{E}[e^{\sigma W_t}]

Substituting the Gaussian moment \mathbb{E}[e^{\sigma W_t}] = e^{\sigma^2 t/2}, which follows by completing the square in the \mathcal{N}(0, t) density,

\mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0\, e^{\mu t}

The level grows at the full rate \mu even as the typical log-return grows at \mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2.

So log-returns have mean (\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\, t and variance \sigma^2 t — variance linear in time (characteristic of Brownian motion), so the standard deviation grows like \sigma\sqrt{t}. Equivalently, the price S_t itself is lognormally distributed: its logarithm is Gaussian, which forces S_t > 0 always — essential, because stock prices can’t go negative.

The -\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 term is the Itô correction in action (Figure 8). Naive chain-rule reasoning would give d(\log S) = dS/S = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW — missing the -\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\, dt contribution that the (dW)^2 = dt rule supplies. The mean of the log-return is therefore not \mu\, t but (\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\, t; the gap is sometimes referred to in finance as the volatility drag.

2.4.2 Solving the OU process

The OU process Equation 11 is the mean-reverting counterpart, and the same lemma determines its long-run law. We solve it in closed form and recover the stationary distribution Equation 12.

2.4.2.1 Use Itô to get reduced SDE

The SDE: The OU process Equation 11 is

dX_t \;=\; \kappa\,(\bar\mu - X_t)\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, dW_t

Centering on its long-run mean, Z_t = X_t - \bar\mu, so that the SDE becomes

dZ_t \;=\; -\kappa\, Z_t\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, dW_t

Itô’s lemma: For a transform f(Z_t, t) of a process with drift coefficient a and diffusion coefficient b — that is, dZ_t = a\, dt + b\, dW_t — the lemma Equation 13 reads

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; a\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial Z} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, b^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial Z^2}\right) dt \;+\; b\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial Z}\, dW

Integrating factor: The standard technique for a linear SDE is to apply Itô’s lemma to the transform Y_t = f(Z_t, t) with f(Z, t) = e^{\kappa t} Z — chosen so the explicit-time term cancels the drift.

Coefficients (from the centered SDE): a = -\kappa\, Z_t and b = \sigma.

Partials (from f = e^{\kappa t} Z):

\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;=\; \kappa\, e^{\kappa t} Z, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial Z} \;=\; e^{\kappa t}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial Z^2} \;=\; 0

Substituting a = -\kappa\, Z, b = \sigma, and the three partials into the lemma,

d\!\left(e^{\kappa t} Z_t\right) \;=\; \Big(\kappa\, e^{\kappa t} Z \;+\; (-\kappa\, Z)\, e^{\kappa t} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 \cdot 0\Big) dt \;+\; \sigma\, e^{\kappa t}\, dW_t

Simplifying — the explicit-time term \kappa\, e^{\kappa t} Z and the drift term -\kappa\, e^{\kappa t} Z cancel,

d\!\left(e^{\kappa t} Z_t\right) \;=\; \sigma\, e^{\kappa t}\, dW_t

2.4.2.2 Solve reduced SDE by integration

Integrating from 0 to t,

\int_0^t d\!\left(e^{\kappa s} Z_s\right) \;=\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{\kappa s}\, dW_s

Evaluating the left side, \int_0^t d\!\left(e^{\kappa s} Z_s\right) = e^{\kappa t} Z_t - Z_0,

e^{\kappa t} Z_t \;=\; Z_0 \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{\kappa s}\, dW_s

As Z_0 = X_0 - \bar\mu,

e^{\kappa t} Z_t \;=\; (X_0 - \bar\mu) \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{\kappa s}\, dW_s

Dividing by e^{\kappa t},

Z_t \;=\; (X_0 - \bar\mu)\, e^{-\kappa t} \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{-\kappa(t - s)}\, dW_s

Substituting Z_t = X_t - \bar\mu,

\boxed{X_t \;=\; \bar\mu \;+\; (X_0 - \bar\mu)\, e^{-\kappa t} \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{-\kappa(t - s)}\, dW_s} \tag{16}

2.4.2.3 Properties of the solution distribution

Given X_0, the offset \bar\mu + (X_0 - \bar\mu)e^{-\kappa t} is a deterministic constant, and the Itô integral is Gaussian by Equation 7; adding the constant leaves X_t an affine function of that Gaussian, and an affine function of a Gaussian is Gaussian.

Mean: The Itô integral has zero mean by Equation 7, so

\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X_t] \;=\; \bar\mu \;+\; (X_0 - \bar\mu)\, e^{-\kappa t}} \tag{17}

Variance: By Equation 7 with g(s) = \sigma\, e^{-\kappa(t - s)},

\operatorname{Var}[X_t] \;=\; \sigma^2 \int_0^t e^{-2\kappa(t - s)}\, ds

Evaluating the integral,

\boxed{\operatorname{Var}[X_t] \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}\big(1 - e^{-2\kappa t}\big)} \tag{18}

Stationary distribution: As t \to \infty the decaying exponentials vanish — e^{-\kappa t} \to 0 in the mean and e^{-2\kappa t} \to 0 in the variance — so \mathbb{E}[X_t] \to \bar\mu and \operatorname{Var}[X_t] \to \sigma^2/(2\kappa). Since X_t is Gaussian for every t, its law converges to

\boxed{\mathcal{N}\!\left(\bar\mu,\;\, \frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}\right)}

which is Equation 12. \square

3 Itô’s Lemma Derives the Black-Scholes Equation

With Itô’s lemma established — and already applied to GBM in Section 2.4.1 — we now turn it to the problem it was developed for: pricing a derivative on a traded stock. We keep the same GBM stock model Equation 10, apply the same lemma to an option’s value V(S,t), and then hedge away the dW exposure with a position in the stock; the random part cancels and a deterministic PDE results — the Black-Scholes equation, in which r is the risk-free rate defined in Section 3.2:

\boxed{\,\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + r S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2} = r V\,} \tag{19}

The rest of this part derives it.

3.1 What is an option?

An option is a contract whose value depends on — is derived from — the price of an underlying stock S_t. The contract grants its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an agreed quantity of the stock at a pre-agreed price per share (strike, K) at a specified maturity (T). The two basic types are:

  • Call option: Confers its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy an agreed quantity of the stock at the strike price K at maturity T.
  • Put option: Confers its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell an agreed quantity of the stock at the strike price K at maturity T.

American options can be exercised at any time up to maturity T while European options can be exercised only at the maturity T. This post restricts attention to European options; American options require additional theory beyond the present scope.

Payoff at expiry: At t = T, the option’s value depends only on S_T. A rational holder exercises the option only when doing so is profitable, giving the piecewise-linear payoff functions:

The call payoff is

\boxed{V_{\text{call}}(S_T) = \max(S_T - K,\, 0)} \tag{20}

The holder exercises if S_T > K, gaining S_T - K; otherwise the option expires worthless.

The put payoff is

\boxed{V_{\text{put}}(S_T) = \max(K - S_T,\, 0)} \tag{21}

The holder exercises if S_T < K, gaining K - S_T; otherwise the option expires worthless.

The kinked “hockey-stick” shape (Figure 9) is the structural signature of an option: identically zero on the unfavourable side of the strike, linear on the favourable side.

3.2 Key finance terms

  • Risk-free rate: The interest rate an investor can expect to earn on an investment that carries zero risk. In practice, usually the interest paid on a 10-year highly rated government Treasury note.
  • Risky asset: An instrument whose future price is uncertain, evolving stochastically. In other words, the diffusion coefficient \sigma(x, t) in its dynamics will not be 0. For example, a stock.
  • Risk-free asset: An instrument whose return is known in advance, carrying no price uncertainty. In other words, the diffusion coefficient \sigma(x, t) in its dynamics will be 0. For example, a bank account; a unit of cash held in it grows deterministically at the risk-free rate.
  • Long / short positions: Holding +q units of an instrument is being long q; owing q units (selling now, buying back later) is being short q (a negative position, -q). A long position profits when the price rises; a short position profits when it falls.
  • Portfolio: A collection of financial investments such as stocks, bonds, and options. If a portfolio has i = 1, \dots, n instruments and the quantity and price of the ith instrument are q_i and P_i respectively, the portfolio value \Pi_t (the symbol is standard in finance, and unrelated to the partition \Pi of Part 1) is \Pi_t = \sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i\, P_i
  • Delta: The sensitivity of an instrument’s value to a one-unit change in the stock price — the partial derivative of that value with respect to S.
  • Portfolio delta: The sensitivity of the portfolio value to a one-unit change in the stock price, \partial \Pi / \partial S. Distributing the partial derivative through the sum, \frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial S} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i\, \frac{\partial P_i}{\partial S}
  • Delta-neutral: A portfolio with zero portfolio delta, \partial \Pi / \partial S = 0 — the quantities q_i are chosen so the deltas of the instruments held cancel, leaving no delta exposure, so the portfolio is immune to a change in the stock price to first order.
  • Self-financing strategy: A trading approach where a portfolio’s value changes only due to gains or losses from its assets, with no external cash inflows or withdrawals.

3.3 The option value process

Given the terminal payoff of Equation 20 as the boundary condition, pricing the option requires finding the SDE its value obeys — and Itô’s lemma provides it, applied to V(S, t) under the same GBM stock dynamics we used for \log S in Section 2.4.1.

Let V(S, t) denote the per-share value of a European call option on S with strike K and maturity T. (Real option contracts typically represent multiple shares; the pricing is done per share throughout this derivation and scales linearly with quantity.) Assume V is twice continuously differentiable in S and once in t for t < T — the hypothesis of Equation 13; the closed-form solution of Section 3.7.1 confirms it for the call, the payoff’s kink at S = K smoothing out instantly for t < T. Apply Itô’s lemma to V under the GBM dynamics of Equation 10 (constant drift \mu, constant volatility \sigma):

dV = \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + \mu S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt + \sigma S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\, dW_t \tag{22}

The challenge that Black-Scholes addresses is the prior question: given today’s price S_t and the stock-price dynamics, what is the fair value V(S_t, t) of the option before expiry, for t < T? Itô’s lemma combined with a delta-neutral, risk-free portfolio of the stock and the option produces a PDE for V whose boundary condition is the terminal call payoff V(S, T) = \max(S - K,\, 0) (Equation 20).

3.4 Black-Scholes assumptions

The Black-Scholes derivation [11], [12] rests on a specific set of idealizing assumptions about the market and the assets traded in it. Collecting them upfront makes both the construction and its limitations transparent.

3.4.1 Market structure

The market consists of two instruments:

  • A risk-free asset — a bank account or zero-coupon bond.
  • A risky asset — a single stock with price S_t.

3.4.2 Assumptions on the assets

  • Risk-free asset dynamics: The risk-free asset B_t earns a continuously-compounded rate r that does not vary with time, dB_t = r\, B_t\, dt Being risk-free, its diffusion term is 0 — there is no dW_t — so its value grows deterministically as B_t = B_0\, e^{rt}.
  • Stock dynamics: The stock price follows the GBM dynamics of Equation 10, with constant drift \mu and constant volatility \sigma, dS_t = \mu\, S_t\, dt + \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t Here the diffusion term is not 0: the \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t term is the source of the stock’s uncertainty, and is what makes it risky.
  • No dividends: The stock pays no dividends over [t, T].

3.4.3 Assumptions on the market

  • No arbitrage: No strategy delivers a risk-free profit in excess of r. In particular, any two portfolios with identical payoffs in every future scenario must have identical prices today.
  • Frictionless trading: Transactions are executed instantaneously with no fees, no bid–ask spread, no taxes, and no market impact. Continuous-time trading is permitted.
  • Unlimited borrowing and lending at r: Cash may be borrowed or lent in any real-valued amount at the risk-free rate.
  • Unrestricted stock positions: Any real-valued quantity of the stock may be held, including short positions (negative quantities), with no borrowing cost or quantity constraint.

The assumptions above are idealizations — real markets violate every one of them to some degree. Their utility is conceptual: under these conditions, the derivative-pricing problem reduces to a well-posed PDE with a known closed-form solution.

3.5 Black-Scholes pricing strategy

Given a European option with terminal payoff V(S, T) = \max(S - K,\, 0) (Equation 20) and the option-value SDE Equation 22, the remaining argument unfolds in three steps:

  1. Form a hedged portfolio: Construct a portfolio by holding +1 unit of the call option and -\Delta_t units of the stock, where \Delta_t = \partial V / \partial S is the option’s delta (Section 3.2), giving \Pi_t = V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t\, S_t The dW_t contributions from dV and from \Delta_t\, dS_t cancel exactly, rendering the portfolio instantaneously risk-free. (Section 3.6)
  2. Invoke no-arbitrage: A risk-free portfolio must earn the risk-free rate: d\Pi_t = r\, \Pi_t\, dt. Equating this with the deterministic dynamics from Step 1 yields a PDE for V(S, t) — the Black-Scholes PDE. (Section 3.7)
  3. Solve the PDE: Solving the PDE using the boundary condition V(S, T) = \max(S - K,\, 0) (Equation 20) gives the Black-Scholes pricing formula for a European call.

3.6 The hedging portfolio

We want to hold the option together with something else so that the combined position is delta-neutral — its value insensitive to small moves in the stock price. Of the other instruments in the market, the risk-free asset has zero delta and cannot offset S-exposure, so the stock is the only candidate: hold the option long and a quantity q_t of the stock, with q_t to be determined:

\Pi_t = V(S_t, t) + q_t\, S_t

Its portfolio delta is the sensitivity of \Pi_t to the stock price, computed from this definition (treating q_t as constant in S at the instant t):

\frac{\partial \Pi_t}{\partial S} = \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + q_t \tag{23}

Delta-neutrality requires \partial \Pi_t/\partial S = 0, which forces q_t = -\partial V/\partial S = -\Delta_t. Thus, the delta-neutral and risk-free portfolio is

\Pi_t = V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t S_t \tag{24}

Over an infinitesimal interval, the portfolio changes by

d\Pi_t = dV - \Delta_t\, dS_t

Writing it this way drops the -S_t\, d\Delta_t - d\Delta_t\, dS_t terms that the Itô product rule adds for a time-varying \Delta_t. This is not an approximation: the hedge is run as a self-financing strategy, so the cash released or absorbed by rebalancing the stock position is exactly offset by a cash account and nets to zero in d\Pi_t over [t, t+dt] — the accounting is in Appendix A.3.

Step 1 — substitute the option change:

Substituting Equation 22 (Itô’s lemma applied to V) for dV,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\, dW_t \;-\; \Delta_t\, dS_t

Step 2 — substitute the stock change:

Substituting Equation 10, dS_t = \mu S\, dt + \sigma S\, dW_t,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\, dW_t \;-\; \Delta_t\, \mu S\, dt \;-\; \Delta_t\, \sigma S\, dW_t

Step 3 — collect like differentials:

Grouping the dt terms and the dW_t terms,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;-\; \Delta_t\, \mu S \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \left(\sigma S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;-\; \Delta_t\, \sigma S\right) dW_t

Step 4 — factor the paired terms:

Factoring \mu S out of the drift pair and \sigma S out of the dW_t pair,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial S} - \Delta_t\right) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma S \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial S} - \Delta_t\right) dW_t

The same factor \big(\partial V/\partial S - \Delta_t\big) now multiplies both the \mu-dependent drift and the entire dW_t exposure.

Step 5 — substitute the hedge:

Substituting \Delta_t = \partial V/\partial S (the position q_t = -\Delta_t chosen above), both parentheses vanish at once,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \tag{25}

Vanishing of the first parentheses means that the expected return of the stock (\mu) has disappeared from the hedged portfolio’s dynamics, meaning the option’s fair value doesn’t depend on it. This implies that two investors who disagree about the stock’s expected return still agree on the option’s price (provided they agree on the volatility \sigma and the risk-free rate r).

Similarly, vanishing of the second parentheses means that d\Pi_t has become independent of dW_t randomness entirely. So the same position choice q_t = -\Delta_t creates a portfolio that is delta-neutral and dW_t-free.

This is the crux of the construction. In Equation 22 the term \sigma S\, \partial V / \partial S\, dW_t made dV random; Equation 25 has no dW_t term at all. A position whose return depended on the random fluctuations of S_t is rendered instantaneously risk-free, and the exposure was hedged away by adding a short stock position to our portfolio.

3.7 The Black-Scholes equation

Because the hedged portfolio \Pi_t has no random component over [t, t+dt], we invoke the no-arbitrage condition and assert that it must earn the risk-free rate r — otherwise there would be a risk-free arbitrage. Thus:

d\Pi_t \;=\; r\, \Pi_t\, dt \tag{26}

Substituting the portfolio definition \Pi_t = V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t\, S_t from Equation 24,

d\Pi_t \;=\; r\, \big[\, V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t\, S_t \,\big]\, dt

Using \Delta_t = \partial V/\partial S,

d\Pi_t \;=\; r\, \left[\, V \;-\; S_t\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \,\right] dt

Equating the drift above with the drift from Equation 25,

\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2} = r V - r S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}

Rearranging gives,

\boxed{\,\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + r S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2} = r V\,}

which is Equation 19. \square

It is worth pausing on what we have arrived at. This is the Black-Scholes equation, published by Fischer Black and Myron Scholes in 1973 [11] and, in the same year, set on a more general footing by Robert Merton [12]. It was the first time anyone had shown that a derivative could be priced by replication — that the option’s risk could be hedged away entirely, leaving a fair value fixed by no-arbitrage alone, independent of any investor’s risk appetite or view on the stock’s expected return. Its impact was immediate and enduring: it gave traders a closed-form price and a hedge ratio they could act on, and the derivatives markets that grew on top of it became among the largest in the world. In 1997 the work was recognized with the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, awarded to Scholes and Merton [13]; Black, who had died in 1995, could not share it, as the prize is not awarded posthumously, though the committee named his role explicitly.

For our purposes the equation is a landmark of a different kind: its second-order term \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2\,\partial_S^2 V — the one that distinguishes it from a deterministic pricing equation — traces back to the single rule (dW)^2 = dt — the same rule we are about to carry into diffusion models.

3.7.1 Solution to the Black-Scholes equation

With the boundary condition V(S, T) = \max(S - K, 0) (Equation 20) for a European call, this PDE has the famous closed-form solution

\boxed{V(S, t) = S\, N(d_1) - K e^{-r(T-t)} N(d_2)} \tag{27}

where N(\cdot) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF) and

d_1 = \frac{\log(S/K) + (r + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)(T-t)}{\sigma\sqrt{T-t}}, \quad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T-t}

Solving the PDE (via change of variables to the heat equation) is a textbook exercise [14]; a step-by-step sketch is in Appendix A.2. The derivation we care about is everything up to the PDE.

3.8 What the derivation establishes

The derivation has a clear logical structure:

  1. We started with an SDE for S_t (the stock price).
  2. We considered a function of that SDE: V(S, t) (the option value).
  3. Itô’s lemma yielded the SDE for V.
  4. The dW term in dV was hedgeable — we could remove the random component with a \Delta-position in the stock.
  5. The hedged portfolio’s drift must match the risk-free rate, yielding a PDE for V.

The Itô correction term — \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \partial_S^2 V — survives the hedging and becomes the second-order term in the PDE. Geometrically, it is the contribution of the option value’s curvature in S — the second derivative \partial_S^2 V, known in finance as the option’s gamma — weighted by the variance rate \sigma^2 S^2.

This structural fact is central: the second-order term in the Black-Scholes PDE comes directly from (dW)^2 = dt. The same pattern appears in Part 4.

4 Itô’s Lemma Transforms DDPM’s Forward Process Twice

Part 3 applied Itô’s lemma once — to the option value V(S, t) — to get an SDE for V, which hedging turned into the Black-Scholes PDE. Part 4 keeps the lemma but puts two different questions to it about the DDPM forward SDE — the two patterns of Section 2.3:

  • Pattern A — given the forward SDE, apply Itô to an integrating factor that collapses its drift; integrating the resulting driftless process gives a closed-form Gaussian law — the perturbation kernel for the noised state x_t given x_0. (Section 4.9)
  • Pattern B — given the forward SDE, derive a PDE for the probability density p(x, t). Applying Itô to a test function and taking expectations turns the SDE into the Fokker-Planck equation, the PDE that governs how the forward process spreads the data density into noise over time. (Section 4.10)

Like Black-Scholes, the first application ends in a closed-form result; but that result is a distribution — the Gaussian law of x_t \mid x_0 — reached by integrating a driftless SDE, rather than a price reached by solving a PDE. Because the transform is linear in x, the second-order Itô term vanishes — and the remaining terms cancel to leave a driftless process — so no analogue of the Black-Scholes second-order term arises.

The second application echoes the Black-Scholes pricing derivation more closely; it too produces a PDE carrying the same second-order term that traces back to (dW)^2 = dt. Where it diverges is in the details: it reaches that PDE indirectly — through a test function and expectations — to govern a density p(x, t) rather than a value V(S, t).

Throughout Part 4, the data x_0, the injected noise, and the state x_t are vectors in \mathbb{R}^d, and I denotes the d \times d identity matrix. The scalar Itô calculus of Parts 1–3 applies componentwise, so the algebra below is written in one dimension.

4.1 What is a generative model?

Under a probabilistic framework, an observed dataset D can be considered a finite set of samples from an underlying unknown data distribution p_0. The goal of a generative model is to approximate this distribution by learning from the dataset D, so that the learned model can be used for inference, e.g. sampling.

4.1.1 Learning

To approximate the distribution parametrically, we need three elements (Figure 10): a model family \mathcal{M} = \{p_\theta\} parameterized by \theta, an objective d(\cdot), and an optimization procedure that minimizes d(\cdot) [15], [16]. Generative learning is then the task of finding the optimal parameters \theta under that procedure, so that the objective d(\cdot) between the true data distribution p_0 and the model distribution p_\theta is minimized.

4.1.2 Inference

Once trained, a generative model answers three inference queries [15], [16]:

  • Density estimation: Given x, return its density p_\theta(x).
  • Sampling: Generate new data x_{\text{new}} \sim p_\theta.
  • Representation learning: Extract meaningful features of x.

Not every model family supports all three efficiently; the trade-offs drive the diversity of generative approaches.

4.2 What are diffusion models?

Diffusion models are a class of latent-variable generative models [2] — models that generate data through unobserved intermediate variables, here the noised states x_1, \ldots, x_N. A diffusion model has two components: the forward process and the reverse process. The forward process progressively adds noise to the training data until nothing but noise remains. The reverse process learns to undo that noising. Sampling starts from noise and runs the learned reverse process, producing new data such as images that resemble the training data.

Two parallel approaches to diffusion models developed independently, differing primarily in the objective d(\cdot): evidence lower bound (ELBO) and score matching. The variational track minimizes the negative ELBO on the data log-likelihood. It runs from Sohl-Dickstein et al.’s nonequilibrium-thermodynamics formulation [17] to Ho et al.’s DDPM [2], where the bound is reparameterized as noise prediction. The score-based track minimizes a score-matching objective. It runs from Hyvärinen’s score matching [18] through Vincent’s denoising score matching [19] to Song and Ermon’s noise-conditional score network [20]. Song et al. merged the two into a single framework in 2021 [1]. Figure 11 places these landmarks on a common timeline.

The table maps each component of the generative-modeling framework to two key diffusion papers.

where

  • \beta_i: The noise schedule, defined in the Definitions section below.
  • \mu_\theta, \sigma_i^2: The learned reverse step’s mean and its pre-fixed variance.
  • \alpha_i: \alpha_i = 1 - \beta_i, the fraction of the previous state’s variance retained at step i.
  • \bar\alpha_i: The cumulative product, \bar\alpha_i = \prod_{j \le i}(1-\beta_j).
  • \epsilon_\theta: The network’s noise estimate.
  • f, g: The forward SDE’s drift and diffusion coefficients — not the transform f of Part 2.
  • s_\theta(x,t): The estimated score \nabla_x \log p_t.
  • d\bar W: The increment of a reverse-time Brownian motion — the reverse-time SDE is post #3’s subject.
  • \mu(t), \Sigma(t): The kernel mean factor and covariance — the kernel mean is \mu(t)\,x_0 — which solve linear ODEs in f and g.
  • \lambda(t): \lambda : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}, a positive weighting function.
  • SGD: Stochastic gradient descent.
  • PF-ODE: The probability-flow ODE (ordinary differential equation).
  • Ancestral sampling: Sampling the learned reverse steps in sequence, i = N, \ldots, 1 — the procedure of the Sampling subsection below.
  • Reverse diffusion: A discretization of the reverse-time SDE, taking one noisy step per time increment.
  • Predictor-Corrector (PC): A reverse-time-SDE step followed by score-based corrector steps at the same noise level.
  • Invertible PF-ODE latent: The ODE is deterministic and reversible, so each x_0 maps to a unique endpoint that maps back to it; that endpoint serves as a latent code, and the change-of-variables formula along the flow turns it into an exact \log p_\theta(x_0).

Each stochastic gradient step samples a fresh triple: a data point x_0 \sim p_0, a step index i (uniform over 1,\dots,N) or a time t (uniform over [0,1]), and a noise vector \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I).

4.3 Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models

Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) [2] are discrete-time diffusion models with roots in nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Like other diffusion models they generate new samples through one central idea: learn to undo noise. If a model can take a slightly noisy sample and remove a small amount of the noise, then, starting from pure noise and applying this repeatedly, it recovers a clean sample (Figure 12).

4.3.1 Forward process (noising)

A fixed, parameter-free procedure that takes a data sample x_0 \sim p_0 and progressively adds Gaussian noise to it, producing a sequence x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_N in which each x_i is a noisier version of x_{i-1} and the endpoint x_N is close to pure noise — a sample from a fixed, data-independent distribution (Figure 13). How much noise enters at each step is set by a noise schedule. This forward process is not an analogy to a diffusion; it is one.

The forward process yields two outputs: for training, clean–noised sample pairs; for inference, pure noise.

4.3.2 Reverse process (denoising)

A learned procedure, usually implemented using neural networks, that starts from pure noise and removes noise step by step, running the forward process in reverse to produce a new sample from p_0. As shown in the table above, each learned reverse step is modeled as a Gaussian distribution whose variance is fixed beforehand, and the only entity to predict is its mean \mu_\theta. Reparameterizing converts the mean-prediction problem into a noise-prediction problem, and \epsilon_\theta is what the network learns to predict. Once the \epsilon_\theta estimate is in hand, \mu_\theta is computed deterministically. That mean, along with the pre-fixed \sigma_i, is used to sample a slightly denoised version of its input. Each reverse step is trained to invert the corresponding forward step. On a training pair the final step x_1 \to x_0 is fitted to return that training sample. At sampling time the same chain, started from a fresh noise sample, produces a new x_0, which is what generation needs.

Note that during actual training, instead of N sequential steps, i is fed to the network as an input, so a single network represents all N reverse steps and each gradient step trains one of them at random. The sequencing lives in the conditioning, not in a loop.

4.3.3 Sampling

The forward process is set up so that x_N has a known, simple distribution we can sample from directly — a standard Gaussian in this case. To generate new data, we sample a noise vector from this distribution and run the reverse process: if the network has learned to undo a single step of the noising process, applying those steps in sequence turns noise into data.

Note that during sampling, unlike training, we take N sequential steps i = N, N-1, \ldots, 1. At each step, the current x_i and i are fed to the network, which outputs the estimated noise \epsilon_\theta for that step. Like training, that \epsilon_\theta is used to compute \mu_\theta, and this, along with the fixed \sigma_i, is used to generate a slightly denoised sample from this estimated Gaussian distribution.

4.4 Why convert the discrete DDPM forward process into an SDE

Before getting into how the DDPM forward process becomes an SDE, and how that yields the closed-form perturbation kernel, it is worth asking why the conversion is needed at all. DDPM obtains that kernel directly, by composing Gaussians and induction on the step index. For that one result the discrete argument is shorter, and nothing below improves on it.

The continuous-time route is taken for what it makes available beyond it. The integrating-factor transform applies to any linear SDE, so it yields the perturbation kernel for the Variance-Exploding schedule (post #3), and for any other linear-SDE noise schedule, without repeating the argument — whereas the induction depends on the particular way the Variance-Preserving steps compose.

The SDE is also the object the rest of the theory relies upon: the Fokker-Planck equation, the reverse-time SDE, and the probability-flow ODE with its numerical solvers all start from the continuous-time process, and none of them follows from the inductively obtained kernel.

And it is the same transform already applied to the OU process in Part 2 — the sense in which one lemma serves both derivations.

4.5 Definitions

As discussed in the above section, DDPM is natively discrete, so to convert it to a continuous-time process, we pick the unit interval [0, 1] and divide it into N equal intervals of size 1/N. This maps N discrete steps i = 1, 2, \ldots, N to N time-steps t = 1/N, 2/N, \ldots, 1. As the final step, we take the step count N \to \infty so the per-step time shrinks to an infinitesimal dt and the sequence becomes an SDE. This is why each object below carries two labels: a discrete one indexed by the step number, and a continuous one indexed by time.

  • Partition (N, \Delta t, \tau_i):
    • N: The number of steps.
    • i: The step index, i \in \{0, 1, \ldots, N\}.
    • t: The continuous time, t \in [0, 1].
    • \Delta t: The step size, \Delta t = 1/N.
    • \tau_i: The continuous time corresponding to step i, \tau_i = i/N.
  • Data sample x_0: A clean sample from the data distribution, x_0 \sim p_0, with x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d.
  • State x_i / x_t:
    • The partially-noised version of x_0.
    • x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d in discrete time; x_N is the noisiest state.
    • x_t \in \mathbb{R}^d in continuous time; x_{t=1} is the noisiest state (written with the time explicit, since x_1 denotes the first discrete state).
  • Noise schedule:
    • Noise added at each step, fixed in advance, not learned.
    • \beta_i: The discrete per-step noise variance, \beta_i \in (0, 1) for i = 1, \ldots, N.
    • \beta(t): The continuous-time noise-variance rate, a continuous function \beta : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty) — over an interval dt the injected noise has variance \beta(t)\, dt.
    • \alpha_i: Defined as \alpha_i = 1 - \beta_i, the fraction of the previous state’s variance retained at step i.
  • Cumulative product \bar\alpha_i / \bar\alpha(t):
    • It is the fraction of the original data variance still present at step i in the discrete case and time t in the continuous case.
    • \bar\alpha_i: The discrete cumulative product \bar\alpha_i := \prod_{s=1}^{i} \alpha_s.
    • \bar\alpha(t): The continuous cumulative product \bar\alpha(t) := \exp\!\big(-\!\int_0^t \beta(s)\, ds\big).
  • Injected noise:
    • \epsilon_i: The noise added at step i, \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) i.i.d., independent of x_0.
    • \epsilon: The standardized accumulation of the injected noise — the total noise in x_i equals \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_i}\,\epsilon in distribution, with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) (a different such variable for each i).
  • Forward transition p(x_i \mid x_{i-1}):
    • The conditional distribution of x_i given x_{i-1}: p(x_i \mid x_{i-1}) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{1 - \beta_i}\, x_{i-1},\ \beta_i I\big)
    • It transforms x_{i-1} into x_i by contracting the previous state by \sqrt{1 - \beta_i} and adding Gaussian noise of variance \beta_i.
    • Equivalently, in reparameterized form: x_i = \sqrt{1 - \beta_i}\, x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta_i}\, \epsilon_i
    • The whole forward process is the chain of these transitions.
  • Discrete perturbation kernel p(x_i \mid x_0):
    • The conditional distribution of the noised state given x_0, obtained by composing the forward transitions and marginalizing out the intermediate states — Gaussian in closed form, derived by induction in Appendix A.7: p(x_i \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_i;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_i) I\big)
    • It produces x_i from x_0 directly by scaling the data by \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i} and adding Gaussian noise of variance 1 - \bar\alpha_i.
    • Equivalently, in reparameterized form: x_i = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\, \epsilon which lets us sample x_i for any i without iterating through the intermediate steps.
  • Continuous perturbation kernel p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0):
    • The continuous-time counterpart, likewise Gaussian in closed form, derived with Itô’s lemma in Section 4.9: p_{0t}(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_t;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha(t)) I\big)
    • It produces x_t from x_0 directly by scaling the data by \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} and adding Gaussian noise of variance 1 - \bar\alpha(t).
